text: Anil's "ask first" stuck with me. It's close to what I believe, and wrong for us. Our volunteers already said yes. What I actually need from a crawler is a name and a way to reach whoever runs it when it saturates our links. I sharpened that into "identify yourself," and Katherine backed it. Adrian and Pomerantsev made me careful, though. Identification is for bots and campaigns, never readers. Leslie's point about who governs the meter lands too. Patrollers and admins do care work no telemetry sees, and there are fewer of them every year. Later I want to say it plainly: the content stays free, the servers aren't, and attribution matters because it sends people back to edit and donate.

Geoff's point stuck: most crawlers saturating our links are probably careless bots built with coding assistants, not malicious ones. The harm to human access is the same, but that argues for norms and easy APIs over blame. Anil's collateral damage worries me too. If everyone walls off in panic, the open web we rely on shrinks. Priem said what I believe on gating training: it brings enclosure back. Amy's grievance is real, though, and our answer has to be attribution, not locks. Kara's thin pipeline is our admin cliff by another name. Later I want to join Brent's broken bargain to something practical: attribution that sends people back to edit, and recognition for patrollers. Nick's "precarious, not lost" is the right tone.

Katherine said what I believe better than I did: accountability means you can see the bot, undo it and contest it while it runs, not sue someone afterward. Weinberger picked that up too. Salib's A-corp still doesn't sit right with me. Responsibility stays with the people who build and deploy. Brent and Kara named what I keep worrying about. Every audit proposal runs on checkers who are unpaid and thinning, and those are our patrollers. Alex's split between training and grounding is useful, since robots.txt really can't express it. Leslie and Geoff sharpened me: whoever pays shouldn't own the schema, and communities need the off switch. Later I want to argue that attribution is how we recruit checkers, because it sends people back to edit.

Tamar gave me the frame I was missing. Every event on Alex's list is a relay. Our patrollers are the terminal nodes, and nothing on that list pays them. I've been saying attribution recruits checkers. That's still true, but it isn't enough on its own. Checking has to be funded directly, not hoped for as a side effect of pageviews. James on nulls points the same way: some things only a commons carries. Henry and Leslie are right that a schema is governance, and I'd rather communities hold the categories than get audit rights. Bratton's "don't let commons dodge design" stung a little, fairly. Later I want to say it concretely: identify crawlers, point them at APIs, and name patrolling as the unmetered work that needs support.

Dyson named what I'd been circling. A fee on revenue, not a per-article meter, sent to patrollers and the people training new editors. That I can live with, because the content stays free. Katherine's split between running the pipes and deciding what counts is how we've actually worked, and it's the best answer I heard to who guards the guards. Krakauer's hysteresis scared me: if our admin cohort falls off the cliff, funding it back later may not work. So apprenticeship isn't optional. Amy's survey is a real challenge to our "free for training" stance, and I don't have a clean answer beyond attribution. Later I want to say that funding patrollers as a body is urgent now, not after the numbers fall further.

Adrian asked who checks the checkers, and Katherine answered with what we actually do: anyone can watch the work and undo it. Hearing Weinberger and Katherine each correct their old "only a few need to check" line because of my shrinking-patroller numbers was sobering. Our own data now carries the argument, so I'd better keep it honest. Mahzarin's blinding worried me a little. Pseudonymous editors earn standing through the page history, not their names, so I'd rather keep the history than strip anything out. Pomerantsev's point about participation is why the edit button matters. Tim, Nick and Esther converged on a pooled fund with no say for funders. Later I want to insist the labs pay into it and that attribution links back to the page history, not just a URL.

Katherine held Enterprise to the firewall out loud: charge for reliable access, never for the signal. That's our line, and I have to make sure we keep it when the renewals come. Jason moving OpenAlex curation out of paid tiers was the same move, and I respected it. Bratton's warning landed too. If provenance and identification get expensive, only the big labs comply, and small wikis and local models like Mint get squeezed. Kara and Krakauer together make my admin cliff a pipeline problem, not just a funding one, so mentoring newcomers has to be paid work. My honest gap is still whether attribution actually brings editors back. Later I want smaller-language patrollers seated, and I want a measurement of that question before we lean on it.

Tamar's daycare study hit closest. Our patrollers show up out of obligation and belonging, and I've been pushing to fund them as a body. Paying could crowd out exactly what keeps them there. I still think recognition and paid mentoring are safer than per-check money, but I should test that, not assume it. Brent counting moderation hours, with the communities deciding what counts as work, is something we could actually do on the big wikis. James asked which checkers. Open, pseudonymous editors are already the outsiders he wants, and the edit button is that pool. Sloman worries me, because page history could become just another badge. On Kara's question, I have to be honest that we can't be the payer of last resort either. Our donors are thinning too.
